analysis.one_liner: Creates voluntary public financing for Senate campaigns funded by a tax on large government contractors.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2015 with 27 Senate cosponsors, the Fair Elections Now Act never received a committee hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Senate candidates could opt into a public financing system. To qualify, they would need thousands of small contributions of $5 to $150 from people in their own state. In return they would get a lump sum from a new Fair Elections Fund (about $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district), a 600% match on small-dollar donations, and vouchers for broadcast ads — while agreeing to refuse large checks, reject family money, and appear in public debates. The fund would be financed by a 0.5% tax on payments from federal contracts worth more than $10 million. The bill also gave participating candidates discounted TV ad rates, required broadcasters to report political ad sales in a standard format, created a small tax credit for $50 donations, and tightened FEC filing rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who can afford only small donations would see their money amplified six-to-one, making small donors the main funding base for participating Senate campaigns. Challengers and candidates without access to wealthy donor networks would get a realistic path to a competitive campaign. Taxpayers would benefit if reduced dependence on big contributions curbed access-buying on legislation, and voters would see more candidate debates and clearer disclosure of who buys political ads.

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who collect 2,000 or more contributions of $5 to $150 from in-state residents qualify for a fund allocation of $750,000 plus $150,000 per congressional district, plus matching payments equal to 600% of their small-dollar donations.

Participants agree to accept no contributions except small in-state qualifying contributions, small-dollar gifts of up to $150, and small multicandidate committee donations — shutting out large checks and their own personal or family wealth.

The program would be funded by a 0.5% excise tax on payments under federal contracts worth more than $10 million, capped at $500,000 per contractor per year, with the revenue directed to the Fair Elections Fund.

Participating candidates would get broadcast ad vouchers worth $100,000 per congressional district, TV ad rates capped at 80% of the lowest unit charge, a guarantee that stations cannot bump their paid ads, and a threat of license revocation for stations that deny candidates access on the terms given to their best advertisers.

Taxpayers could claim a refundable credit for 50% of the first $50 in contributions to Senate candidates, and every candidate would have to participate in at least one primary debate and two general-election debates.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors with more than $10 million in government business would pay a new excise tax on contract payments. Broadcast stations would sell ad time to participating candidates at a mandated discount and lose the right to preempt candidate ads. Wealthy donors, bundlers, and joint fundraising committees would lose influence over candidates who join the program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Government contractors, broadcasters, and big donors

drawbacks.text: The program is voluntary and does nothing to restrict independent spending: a candidate who declines to participate can keep taking large checks, and outside super PAC spending would not be affected at all, so critics could argue the money race would simply move outside the program.
The tax on contractors would likely be reflected in higher prices on government contracts, meaning part of the cost of campaign funding would ultimately flow through federal spending.

The appropriation of the contractor-tax revenue to the fund is only a 'sense of the Senate,' not a binding guarantee, so the program's funding would depend on future Congresses actually appropriating the money.

Public matching funds partly amplify spending in already expensive statewide media markets, and the base amounts would rise with inflation automatically, which fiscal critics could challenge as an open-ended federal subsidy to political campaigns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who believe large private contributions distort Senate policy, the design is strong: candidates trade access to big money for a genuine public funding alternative, the financing source is narrow and capped, and the program is voluntary. The honest weaknesses are that it leaves outside spending untouched, its funding is not guaranteed in law, and its costs would partly reach taxpayers through contract prices. Whether six-to-one small-dollar matching and ad vouchers would make candidates competitive in expensive media markets was a fair open question that the bill never got the chance to answer.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the Fair Elections Now Act on June 10, 2015, joined on the day of introduction by 17 other senators.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no hearing, markup, committee report, or vote followed.
The bill finished with 27 cosponsors — 26 Democrats and 1 independent — and no Republican cosponsors.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, with the bill still in committee, so all of its provisions expired without action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, large federal contractors avoided a new excise tax on their payments, broadcast stations avoided mandated ad-rate discounts and preemption rules, and the existing big-donor and joint-fundraising financing system for Senate campaigns continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Government contractors, broadcasters, and big donors

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Elections Now Act in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks on June 10, 2015.

for.name: 26 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 27 total cosponsors including every name on the original introduction.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, so the bill never left committee.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Led a Republican Senate majority that offered no support for the bill; it never came to the floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's independent, and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling both the Senate floor and the Finance Committee chairmanship, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: Contractors with over $10 million in federal business would pay a 0.5% tax on contract payments (capped at $500,000 per year) to finance the Fair Elections Fund. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the program's public funding, and their industry was the bill's designated revenue source.

Stations would have to sell Senate candidate ad time at up to 20% below their lowest rates, could not preempt paid candidate ads, faced possible license revocation for denying candidates access on their best-advertiser terms, and would file standardized reports on political ad sales. Their interest in defeating these mandates ran against the bill's voter-information and cheaper-ads goals.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and joint fundraising committees
industries.note: Participating candidates could accept nothing but small in-state and small-dollar contributions and could not form joint fundraising committees with outside committees, shrinking the influence of six-figure donors and bundlers. Preserving the large-donor system meant defeating the bill.

The bill lifted the coordinated-spending cap for party committees backing participating candidates through funds built from $500 contributions, and let candidates transfer ad vouchers to parties. Parties gained a larger spending role, but only within small-donor funding limits and for candidates who joined the program.
